A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same DUST research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite reformatting, renumbering, and substantial additions.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoboCasa, GR-1, and Franka experiments, BridgeV2 transfer results, sampling experiments, and component ablations.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds LIBERO/CALVIN evaluations, heterogeneous-data training, additional real-world tasks, latency measurements, and diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed dual-stream MMDiT architecture, independent modality noising, weighted flow-matching objective, and asynchronous Euler sampler remain unchanged. Heterogeneous-data training applies the existing framework; alternative embeddings and zero vision denoising are evaluated as ablations.

E1.justification: V3 adds LIBERO and CALVIN ABC-D evaluation, EgoDex human demonstrations within mixed robot–human training, and three Franka tasks involving cord insertion, erasing, and brushing. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's simulation benchmarks, action-free video pretraining, and four real-world pick-and-place tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond GR00T-N1.5 and FLARE, v3 evaluates π0 and π0-FAST on RoboCasa/GR-1, PAD and VPP in selected demonstration regimes, and π0 on Franka. FLARE is added to the BridgeV2 pretraining comparison. LIBERO/CALVIN tables include further comparators, with results taken from other papers explicitly distinguished from locally reproduced experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include heterogeneous training with batch size 512 for 60k steps, LIBERO/CALVIN training schedules, noisy-future-state conditioning evaluated by action MSE, and RTX 5090/TorchInductor latency benchmarking. Added real-world tasks introduce distinct scoring rules and 24-trial evaluations. Original training budgets remain. V3's GR-1 caption changes the task grouping to 18/6, while its appendix retains 16/8, leaving that description inconsistent.

E4.justification: V3 adds semantic-versus-VAE embedding ablations, action prediction under corrupted future observations, zero-vision-denoising evaluation, latency analysis, and an occlusion-related failure case. Existing architecture, noise, depth, loss-weight, and synchronous-sampling ablations remain. V1's qualitative DUST-versus-GR00T cup-grasp comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, variation across repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; additional real-world trial counts describe evaluation sample sizes without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark and ablation scores match after percentage conversion. New results include LIBERO 96.2% for DUST and FLARE, CALVIN average chain lengths of 3.91 versus 3.75, and mixed-training improvement from 58.5% to 64.4%. The real-world average changes from 67.7% over four tasks to a reported 59.9% over seven, not a same-setting decline. V3's seven printed DUST scores actually average about 60.2%, leaving its aggregate unexplained.

T1.justification: The formal problem setup, interpolation definitions, flow-matching losses, and Euler updates in equations (1)–(5) are substantively retained. Neither version introduces original theorems or proofs. V3's dependency verification is empirical rather than a new formal result.

C1.justification: The central architecture, decoupled-training, and asynchronous-sampling contributions remain. V3 extends the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's transfer-learning claim to heterogeneous robot–human joint training, alongside retained action-free video pretraining, and updates the headline real-world gain for its expanded evaluation.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of heterogeneous transfer, semantic versus reconstructive embeddings, and benefits retained without vision denoising. Section 5.3 explains non-monotonic scaling through accumulated ODE approximation errors. Appendix A.11 newly identifies self-occlusion and reliance on current observations as failure conditions, qualifying v1's predominantly positive account of anticipatory control.

D1.justification: V3 adds benchmark-specific training budgets and hardware, mixed-data batching and hand-pose retargeting details, latency measurement conditions, and a project-page pointer. However, v1's Appendix A.6 training and sampling pseudocode is removed. Core optimizer, encoder, learning-rate, and original training-budget details remain available.

R1.justification: V3 expands positioning to concurrent world-action models, including Cosmos Policy, Fast-WAM, and DreamZero, explicitly distinguishing their video-generation priors from VLA augmentation. It adds optical-flow policy work, MMDiT attribution, and a substantial set of references supporting new VLA comparisons, benchmarks, human data, and representation analyses.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and world-modeling preliminaries receive substantial rewriting. Transfer learning is reorganized into joint-training and pretraining discussions, and the appendix structure changes considerably. Reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed, while acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. The rewritten noise example also introduces endpoint notation inconsistent with the retained equations.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text from single-column to two-column presentation and reworks architecture and sampling diagrams. Comparison tables gain rows and task columns, and new experiment tables and a latency plot are added. The real-world task illustration is relocated and revised, the cup-grasp comparison is removed, and retained rollout illustrations are redistributed.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the proposal: PAD/VPP comparisons test alternatives central to its motivation, while additional benchmarks, insertion/tool-use tasks, latency measurements, and targeted ablations address v1's limited coverage and unmeasured deployment trade-offs. The failure analysis clarifies applicability. Pseudocode removal, notation/task-count inconsistencies, and the Table 3 aggregation discrepancy weaken reproducibility and precision; uncertainty reporting remains absent. These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and diagnostic analysis.
